conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode (bear mirror per Brooks). swingHigh(n)/swingLow(n) = the n-th most recent confirmed swing pivot per T17-01's pivotStrength-bar confirmation; tick = instrument minimum move.

candidates.name: DoubleBottomTopPrimitive
candidates.quote: If a market forms a double bottom after a sell-off, and before the bull trend takes off, and it then has a higher low pullback that tests just above the double bottom low, this is a double bottom pullback long setup. The double bottom does not have to be exact, and the second bottom is often slightly lower than the first.
candidates.description: Primitive: two swing lows within a tolerance of each other's level, separated by an opposing move, form a double bottom (mirrored for a double top). Brooks explicitly does NOT require the two extremes to be equal - the second is often slightly beyond the first.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (pattern classification, feeds an Entry elsewhere)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection plus a toleranced level match between the two most recent same-side pivots

notes: Same underlying primitive as DoubleTopBottomPattern (V01-06); defined independently per chapter per convention, dedup pass should merge.

Brooks: 'Some technicians say triple bottoms/tops always fail... but they require that the three extremes be identical to the tick... traders will make much more money by using loose definitions' - explicit argument for keeping toleranceTicks nonzero rather than requiring an exact match.

candidates.name: DoubleBottomPullbackEntry
candidates.quote: it then has a higher low pullback that tests just above the double bottom low, this is a double bottom pullback long setup... A double bottom (or top) pullback pattern can be thought of as a three-push bottom... where the third push down did not have strong-enough sellers to create a new low.
candidates.description: After a double bottom (V08-01) is followed by a breakout rally and then a third pullback that holds above the double bottom's low (a third push down that fails to make a new low), buy the reversal back up off that third pullback.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the reversal (third-push) signal bar's high

complexity.reason: inherits V08-01's swing-pivot/tolerance detection plus a third-pullback zone test against the double bottom's own level

notes: Brooks: 'When the market forms a double bottom pullback and the shape is good and the bull reversal bars for the three bottoms are strong, especially if the final one is strong, the pattern is one of the most reliable buy setups.'

Also matches when the third push instead ends AT the double-bottom level (a triple bottom) or slightly BELOW it and reverses up (a failed breakout below the double bottom) - Brooks treats all three shapes as the same setup; testZoneTicks/holdMarginTicks are read broadly enough to allow this, but a strict implementation may want a separate signed offset rather than one zone width.

candidates.name: ShallowSecondExtremeDowngradesToScalp
candidates.quote: If the second bottom does not at least reach the first, there is a risk that the bottom is forming only a two-legged sideways to up correction, thereby making it better to look for a scalp long rather than a swing.
candidates.description: If the second extreme of a candidate double bottom fails to reach (stays above) the first extreme's level, treat any resulting long as a scalp-only trade (reduced target, no swing) rather than a full reversal trade, since the move may just be a two-legged sideways-to-up correction instead of a reversal.
candidates.pseudocode:
secondExtremeDidNotReachFirst = swingLow(1) > swingLow(2) + toleranceTicks * tick;
restrictToScalpTarget = secondExtremeDidNotReachFirst

complexity.reason: inherits V08-01's swing-pivot detection; the comparison itself is trivial once the pivots are known

candidates.name: WeakSecondExtremeInStrongTrendNegatesReversal
candidates.quote: bar 3 was 5 cents above the bar 2 low in a very strong bear trend. This slightly higher low usually negates the pattern and makes a two-legged bear rally much more likely than a new bull trend.
candidates.description: When the underlying trend is very strong, a second extreme that fails to reach the first (V08-03) does not just downgrade the trade to a scalp - it more often negates the reversal setup entirely, since a strong trend is more likely to produce only a two-legged with-trend correction than a genuine reversal.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter that can suppress V08-02's entry entirely)

complexity.reason: 'very strong trend' has no stated bar-level test; needs a design decision (e.g. consecutive trend-bar count or EMA-gap measure) before coding

notes: Also restates the chapter's related caveat: 'bottom picking in a strong bear trend without a prior strong trend line break is not a good approach' (p.249), the same trend-line-break precondition as V01-01/VP1-01.

candidates.name: DoubleBottomReversalVsBullFlagContext
candidates.quote: This is a reversal pattern and not a continuation pattern, like the double bottom bull flag. Both are long entry setups, but one is the beginning of the trend (a reversal pattern) and the other takes place in an established trend (a continuation pattern).
candidates.description: The same double-bottom shape (V08-01) is traded identically as a long setup either way, but its classification differs by context: forming at the end of a bear trend (no established bull trend yet) it is a reversal pattern; forming within an already-established bull trend it is a continuation pattern (a double bottom bull flag).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (classification only; both classifications trade the same entry as V08-02)

complexity.reason: depends on classifying whether a trend is 'established', a design decision this corpus repeatedly flags as research-grade (always-in direction)

notes: No difference in the entry trigger itself (V08-02 covers both); this only affects target/hold-time expectations (reversal trades are held for a potential swing, continuation trades are more often scalped, per the surrounding chapters).

candidates.name: DoubleTopAndBottomInSameRangeFormsTriangle
candidates.quote: Sometimes there will be both a double top and a double bottom in the same trading range. The result is usually a triangle, which means that the market is in breakout mode... If the setup is good, the probability of success is about 60 percent for a reward that is at least as large as the risk.
candidates.description: When a trading range contains both a double top and a double bottom (V08-01 fired on both sides), classify it as a triangle in breakout mode: scalp shorts off the double top and longs off the double bottom while the range holds; if it is too tight to scalp, either swing a position from one side or wait for the breakout and trade with a strong breakout (fade it back into the range if the breakout instead fails).
candidates.book_order_type: limit orders to scalp at the range edges; stop entries with the breakout direction; stop entries fading a failed breakout

complexity.reason: requires V08-01's pivot/tolerance detection on both sides of the range plus an undefined breakout-strength test

notes: Brooks gives explicit backtested-sounding probabilities (60% for the range scalps, 70%+ for a strong-breakout continuation) that are not themselves codable as a bar-level test, only the entry/exit logic is.

candidates.name: DoubleBottomFromEntryBarStopRunLevel
candidates.quote: The bottom of an entry bar has protective stops below it and it will often be tested, as it was by bar 2, and two moves down to the same level is a double bottom, even if the first one is not a swing low.
candidates.description: A double bottom's first extreme does not need to be a confirmed swing pivot - the low of any recent entry (signal) bar, which traders' protective stops sit just below, qualifies as the first extreme if a later bar tests down to that same level and holds.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (pattern classification, a looser precondition than V08-01)

complexity.reason: tracking a recent entry bar's own low/high needs only a short persistent memory (not full swing-pivot detection), so it is simpler than V08-01 despite serving the same role

notes: Notable because it is CHEAPER than the general V08-01/T17-01 pivot definition: no confirmation lag is needed since the reference level is a known signal bar's own extreme, not a pivot that requires bars on both sides to confirm.

rejected.quote: it is simply arrogant to tell the market that you will not allow it to do something, and arrogance always costs you money because it is the market and not you that gets to say what can and will happen.
rejected.reason: pure opinion/discretion about trading psychology, no bar-level test

chapter_summary: Chapter 8 treats the double top/bottom pullback as a three-push pattern where the third push fails to make a new extreme (V08-01/V08-02), explicitly arguing for a toleranced (not exact-tick) match between the two extremes. It gives two related degrade rules for when the second extreme falls short of the first: downgrade to a scalp-only target in general (V08-03), or skip the reversal entirely when the underlying trend is very strong (V08-04, research-grade). It draws a reversal-vs-continuation distinction based on whether a bull trend is already established (V08-05, research-grade, same always-in caveat as elsewhere in the corpus), covers the case where a trading range contains both a double top and a double bottom and becomes a triangle in breakout mode with explicit (non-codable) probability figures (V08-06), and loosens the pattern's own definition to allow the first extreme to be an unconfirmed entry-bar low rather than a full swing pivot (V08-07) - a materially cheaper precondition than the T17-01 pivot definition used elsewhere. The chapter's second half (Figures 8.1-8.4, pp.247-252) is entirely worked chart examples; no additional general rules beyond restatements of the above were found there.
